_Implementation details and Datasets._ Our method is implemented
in C++ using the geometry processing library Easy3D [Nan 2021] for
efficient and reliable mesh operations, and CGAL [The CGAL Project
2024] for robust computation of Voronoi diagrams. For evaluation,
we employ both publicly available and self-constructed datasets
for assessment. The public data is sampled from the models in the
Fusion 360 Gallery Dataset [Willis et al. 2021], comprising a total of
100 samples. We create our own test data using FreeCAD [Riegel
et al. 2016]. The self-constructed models include original, unfilleted
versions, which can serve as ground truth for evaluating the performance of fillet removal. All experiments are performed on a desktop
machine equipped with an Intel(R) Core i9-13900K CPU running
at 5.80 GHz and 64 GB of RAM.

which do not require frequent adjustment. The parameters _𝑘_ and _𝜎_ are used to compute _𝜌_ in Eq. (4), with
_𝑘_ = 30 and _𝜎_ = 1 _._ 0 controlling the smoothness of _𝜌_ (larger _𝜎_ yields
smoother results). Due to the density difference between rolling-ball
trajectories and other regions, the algorithm may fail only when _𝜎_
is excessively large. To further reduce sensitivity to _𝜎_, we normalize
the input model to a unit sphere. The weights _𝛽𝑒_ and _𝛽𝑓_ control the energy terms for edge and
face alignment, respectively. Since the number of edges is roughly
proportional to the number of faces, both _𝛽𝑒_ and _𝛽𝑓_ are typically
set to 1. Meanwhile, _𝛽𝑐_ regulates the convergence behavior: a value
too small may lead to non-manifold meshes, while a value too large
may reduce efficiency. Therefore, we typically set _𝛽𝑐_ = 0 _._ 5 for a
good balance. Finally, the remaining parameters— _𝜆_, _𝜖_, _𝑟_ max, and _𝜃_ min—are assigned default values as mentioned earlier.

Fillet identification is the first stage of DeFillet. We select two traditional primitive detection solvers, E-RANSAC [Schnabel et al. 2007]
and QSE [Yan et al. 2012], for comparison, using the same number of samples as our method. Additionally, in recent years, deep
learning has made significant advances in primitive detection. We
also evaluate the fillet identification capabilities of several recent
works, including ParSeNet [Sharma et al. 2020], HPNet [Yan et al. 2021], and SED-Net [Li et al. 2023]. Specifically, we set the distance
threshold of E-RANSAC to 0 _._ 001 and the number of clusters for
QSE to 144. The learning-based methods are used with their default
parameters and sample sizes as recommended by the authors. All
compared methods provide segmentation results, classifying each
point into different primitive types. As shown in Fig. 12, the comparison methods decompose the
surface into cylinders (yellow), cones (purple), spheres (green), and
planes (blue). The torus (E-RANSAC), quadrics (QSE), and B-splines
(ParSeNet, HPNet, SED-Net) are highlighted in red.

5.3 Comparison on Fillet Removal


The objective of this paper is to revert a filleted CAD model to its
original unfilleted state. For comparison, we adopt three featurepreserving shape reconstruction methods: VSR [Zhao et al. 2023],
RFEPS [Xu et al. 2022], and KSR [Bauchet and Lafarge 2020]. While
these methods are not specifically designed for the _DeFillet_ task, they
do possess certain sharpening capabilities. VSR leverages quadric
error metrics (QEM) and variational partitioning to reconstruct
sharp features. RFEPS identifies sharp feature points using Optimal
Transport theory and reconstructs a surface mesh with sharp edges
through a Restricted Power Diagram. KSR, in contrast, first detects
planar primitives to piecewise fit the input point cloud, then extends
these primitives until they collide. The sharp features naturally
emerge at the intersections of these planar primitives. To enhance
their ability to remove fillet regions, we set the split threshold of
VSR to 0 _._ 01 and the _𝑘_ -nearest-neighbor parameter of RFEPS to 50. For KSR, the input point cloud consists of samples from the fillet
regions detected and removed by our method. All methods take 50 _𝑘_
samples as input. ACM Trans. Graph., Vol. 44, No. 4, Article . Publication date: August 2025. As shown in Fig. 13, the model is constructed by FreeCAD [Riegel
et al. 2016] which has different radius of fillets. All competitors
remove fillets with small radius and reconstruct sharp feature.

which the _𝐸𝑒_ and _𝐸𝑓_ energies diminish during the iteration process. As shown in Fig. 18, when _𝛽𝑐_ is small (e.g., 0 _._ 05), the defilleted

Our algorithm demonstrates exceptional defilleting performance on
various CAD objects, as shown in Fig. 20. The input CAD models

models feature varying triangle counts (samples # _𝒮_ ) and diverse

and the total time overhead _𝑇_ . Our algorithm consistently achieves
excellent fillet removal performance across these models. Notably,
model #3 includes fillets with gradually varying radii, while our
algorithm still successfully restores its original shape. The efficiency
of the fillet segmentation step is proportional to the number of
samples, while the efficiency of the removal step is more closely

We compare our proposed fillet radius variation rate with principal
curvature. In certain CAD systems, it is possible to specify the
subdivision count of polygonal fillet surfaces along the principal
curvature direction, referred to as _fillet segments_ . As shown at the
top of Fig. 21, we visualize the absolute value of the maximum
principal curvature and initially set a high fillet segment counts
of 100. It can be observed that the maximum principal curvature
identifies the fillet regions, with fillets of different radii highlighted
in different colors. However, the distinction between the fillet and
non-fillet regions is not very clear. When the fillet segment count
is reduced to 5, the curvature still identifies small-radius fillets but
loses the identification of larger-radius fillets. The distribution of
principal curvature exhibits a striped pattern, as the curvature is
zero within each segment. To ensure the same monotonicity as the
principal curvature, we visualize the field of 1 − _ℛ_ at the bottom
of Fig. 21. It can be seen that the proposed fillet radius variation rate
remains stable across varying radii and segment counts.

Our method accurately identifies Voronoi vertices located along the
fillet rolling ball trajectory and captures the fillet radius, enabling
customized fillet removal. This capability is particularly useful for
applications where selective removal of fillets based on their radius
is offered, such as in the secondary design process where adjustments or refinements to the geometry are needed. This functionality
provides greater flexibility and control in the design and modification of models, making it highly valuable for iterative design
workflows. 5.8 Potential Applications


_A pre-step for primitive detection._ Our algorithm can be applied
to assist in the segmentation of CAD models, which is crucial for
reverse CAD engineering. We perform the quadrics segmentation
software QSE which was developed by Yan et al. [2012] to segment
the model shown on the left of Fig. 23. It can be seen that QSE struggles to achieve a fine segmentation. While increasing the number of
iterations and human interaction might lead to better segmentation
results, it also increases the labor cost. Our method can serve as a
valuable tool in aiding QSE to rapidly achieve reasonable segmentation by incorporating fillet boundary constraints, as depicted on
the right side of Fig. 23. _Secondary Design._ As shown in Fig. 24, our algorithm is capable
of restoring sharp edges from previously filleted areas.

chunks.chunk_section: Abstract
chunks.text:
Title: DeepMill: Neural Accessibility Learning for Subtractive Manufacturing

Authors: Fanchao Zhong *, 
Yang Wang* 
( Shandong University ), Peng-Shuai Wang ( Peking University ), Lin Lu , Haisen Zhao ( Shandong University )
* Equal contribution

Abstract: Abstract Manufacturability is vital for product design and production, with accessibility being a key element, especially in subtractive manufacturing. Traditional methods for geometric accessibility analysis are time-consuming and struggle with scalability, while existing deep learning approaches in manufacturability analysis often neglect geometric challenges in accessibility and are limited to specific model types. In this paper, we introduce DeepMill, the first neural framework designed to accurately and efficiently predict inaccessible and occlusion regions under varying machining tool parameters, applicable to both CAD and freeform models. To address the challenges posed by cutter collisions and the lack of extensive training datasets, we construct a cutter-aware dual-head octree-based convolutional neural network (O-CNN) and generate an inaccessible and occlusion regions analysis dataset with a variety of cutter sizes for network training. Experiments demonstrate that DeepMill achieves 94.7% accuracy in predicting inaccessible regions and 88.7% accuracy in identifying occlusion regions, with an average processing time of 0.04 seconds for complex geometries. Based on the outcomes, DeepMill implicitly captures both local and global geometric features, as well as the complex interactions between cutters and intricate 3D models.

geometric methods, our network significantly reduces computation time, enabling real-time prediction during shape editing. Across various CAD and freeform
model datasets with different mesh resolutions, the accuracy for inaccessible regions and occlusion regions reach 94.7% and 88.7%, respectively. The cutter
sizes for each shape in the figure are randomly generated. We display the cutter shapes used for two shapes. On the left, the red and green areas represent
inaccessible and severely occlusion regions predicted by the network. Dark red (green) and light red (green) areas indicate under- and over-predictions,
respectively, compared to the traditional geometric method. On the right, the results of applying our network for volume accessibility analysis are shown.

1 INTRODUCTION


Manufacturability is a fundamental concept in product design and
production [Gupta et al. 1997; Shukor and Axinte 2009], referring to
the ease and efficiency with which a design can be transformed into
a physical product, while accounting for factors such as material
constraints, cutter capabilities, and production costs [Hoefer et al. 2017; Joshi and Chang 1988; Li and Frank 2006].

5.1 Data processing and datasets

_Data processing and cleaning._ We performed the accessibility and
occlusion analysis described in section 4 to construct the training
and test sets, uniformly sampled 150 cutter directions on the upper
hemisphere. We selected various CAD shapes from the ABC dataset

[Koch et al. 2019] and freeform shapes from Thingi10K [Zhou and
Jacobson 2016]. After cleaning non-manifold, non-watertight, and
multi-component assemblies, we retained high-quality shapes. To
avoid invalid data from shapes significantly smaller than the cutter,
we extracted each shape’s bounding box, ensuring its minimum
edge length was at least 80 mm.

This paper introduces DeepMill, a deep learning framework that
improves cutter accessibility and manufacturability analysis for
complex designs. Utilizing octree-based convolutional neural network (O-CNN), DeepMill efficiently predicts inaccessible regions
and occlusions across various cutter sizes, overcoming the scalability
and computational limitations of traditional methods. Its real-time
predictions enable faster design iterations and enhance production
efficiency. Additionally, the new dataset introduced supports further research and development of robust manufacturability analysis

chunks.text:
Title: Deformable Beta Splatting

Authors: Rong Liu *, Dylan Sun *, 
Meida Chen, Yue Wang , 
Andrew Feng 
( University of Southern California ) 
* Co-first authors

Abstract: Abstract 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has advanced radiance field reconstruction by enabling real-time rendering. However, its reliance on Gaussian kernels for geometry and low-order Spherical Harmonics (SH) for color encoding limits its ability to capture complex geometries and diverse colors. We introduce Deformable Beta Splatting (DBS), a deformable and compact approach that enhances both geometry and color representation. DBS replaces Gaussian kernels with deformable Beta Kernels, which offer bounded support and adaptive frequency control to capture fine geometric details with higher fidelity while achieving better memory efficiency. In addition, we extended the Beta Kernel to color encoding, which facilitates improved representation of diffuse and specular components, yielding superior results compared to SH-based methods. Furthermore, Unlike prior densification techniques that depend on Gaussian properties, we mathematically prove that adjusting regularized opacity alone ensures distribution-preserved Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), independent of the splatting kernel type. Experimental results demonstrate that DBS achieves state-of-the-art visual quality while utilizing only 45% of the parameters and rendering 1.5x faster than 3DGS-based methods. Notably, for the first time, splatting-based methods outperform state-of-the-art Neural Radiance Fields, highlighting the superior performance and efficiency of DBS for real-time radiance field rendering.

1 INTRODUCTION


Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [Barron et al. 2021, 2023; Mildenhall
et al. 2021; Müller et al. 2022] have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in 3D scene representation and novel view synthesis but
are hindered by high computational costs and limited applicability in real-time scenarios due to their reliance on neural networkbased encoding and dense volumetric ray-marching. More recently,
3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [Kerbl et al. 2023] introduced an
explicit representation paradigm that shifts from volumetric raymarching to point-based splatting. By representing scenes as a set
of 3D Gaussian primitives, 3DGS significantly reduces computational overhead, achieving real-time radiance field rendering while
maintaining visual quality comparable to earlier NeRF methods. This explicit representation eliminates the need for heavy neural
networks and enables direct manipulation of scene geometry and
real-time rendering, making 3DGS ideal for applications such as
immersive VR exploration [Franke et al. 2024; Jiang et al. 2024; Yu
et al. 2024], dynamic scene representation [Guo et al. 2024; Luiten
et al. 2023; Wu et al. 2024; Yang et al. 2023, 2024b], 3D content creation [Chung et al. 2023; Tang et al. 2024; Yi et al. 2024a,b], mesh
extraction [Dai et al. 2024; Guédon and Lepetit 2023; Huang et al. 2024; Liu et al.

in efficiency, its rendering quality still falls short of the latest NeRF
advancements [Barron et al. 2023], particularly in capturing fine
details and modeling view-dependent colors. To address this gap, a
range of extensions has emerged, focusing on improving its visual
quality through anti-alising [Liang et al. 2024; Song et al. 2024; Yan
et al. 2024; Yu et al. 2023], deblurring [Lee et al. 2024; Oh et al. 2024;
Peng et al. 2024; Seiskari et al. 2024; Zhao et al. 2024], appearance

have yet to surpass the state-of-the-art NeRF methods [Kulhanek
and Sattler 2024].

have yet to surpass the state-of-the-art NeRF methods [Kulhanek
and Sattler 2024]. The limitations of 3DGS primarily arise from the constraints of
its foundational components. The Gaussian kernel, while enabling
real-time rendering through its explicit representation, inherently
produces smooth and blurred results. This smoothing effect hinders
its ability to accurately depict flat surface geometries and sharp
edges, resulting in a loss of fine detail and diminished realism in
rendered scenes. Additionally, the Gaussian kernel’s long-tailed and
unbounded nature necessitates a hard-coded cut-off for efficient
rendering. This workaround introduces cut-off artifacts and further
compromises the accurate representation of fine geometric details. Furthermore, 3DGS employs low–order Spherical Harmonics (SH) to
encode view-dependent color information. Although SH can model
lighting variations, its parameter count increases polynomially with
the SH level, limiting practical use in real-time applications. As a
result, 3DGS relies on lower SH levels, which inherently produce
smooth and overly simplified color transitions.

Although SH can model
lighting variations, its parameter count increases polynomially with
the SH level, limiting practical use in real-time applications. As a
result, 3DGS relies on lower SH levels, which inherently produce
smooth and overly simplified color transitions. This prevents the
accurate modeling of specular highlights and fails to decouple diffuse
and specular components, resulting in suboptimal representations of
complex lighting interactions. Notably, both Gaussian kernel and SH
are fixed-function mappings, restricting the adaptability required to
handle varying scene complexities and lighting conditions, further
compromising visual fidelity. To address these shortcomings, we propose Deformable Beta
Splatting (DBS), a novel framework designed to enhance both geometric and color representation in radiance field rendering. At the
core of DBS is the Beta Kernel, inspired by the Beta distribution,
which provides bounded support and flexible shape control. This kernel adapts naturally to diverse scene complexities, enabling accurate
representation of flat surfaces, sharp edges, and smooth regions with
high fidelity. For color representation, we introduce the Spherical
Beta (SB) function for view-dependent color encoding. By decoupling diffuse and specular components, SB effectively models sharp
specular reflections and captures high-frequency lighting effects.

For color representation, we introduce the Spherical
Beta (SB) function for view-dependent color encoding. By decoupling diffuse and specular components, SB effectively models sharp
specular reflections and captures high-frequency lighting effects. Compared to spherical harmonics (SH) of degree 3, SB achieves superior performance using only 31% of the parameters, significantly
improving model efficiency. Finally, we revisit and adapt Markov
Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) principles from 3DGS-MCMC [Kheradmand et al. 2024] into the Deformable Beta Splatting framework to
address unique challenges posed by deformable kernels. Specifically,
the adaptive density control in 3DGS and the probability-preserved
densification strategies in 3DGS-MCMC were designed for Gaussian



kernels, making their direct application to deformable Beta kernels
nontrivial. To overcome this, we mathematically prove that by regularizing opacity, adjusting opacity alone is valid for distributionpreserved densification, regardless of the number of densifications
or the choice of splatting kernel. This results in a kernel-agnostic
MCMC strategy, eliminating the need for complex heuristics and
scale recomputation, thereby streamlining both the optimization
and densification processes. Additionally, we redefine the noise function used in MCMC with the Beta kernel to maintain mathematical
consistency and compatibility with opacity constraints.

Additionally, we redefine the noise function used in MCMC with the Beta kernel to maintain mathematical
consistency and compatibility with opacity constraints. The comprehensive experimental results demonstrate that our
approach consistently outperforms both 3DGS-based and NeRFbased methods in visual quality across all benchmarks. Furthermore,
our method utilizes only 45% of the parameters required by 3DGS
and renders 1.5x faster than 3DGS-MCMC, demonstrating DBS’s
superior performance in real-time radiance field rendering. To summarize, the main contributions of our paper are as follows:


(1) Beta Kernel for Geometry Representation: A bounded, flexible kernel that improves geometric fidelity by accurately
capturing flat surfaces, sharp edges, and smooth regions. (2) Spherical Beta for Color Encoding: An efficient view-dependent
color model that decouples diffuse and specular components,
enabling sharp specular highlights with fewer parameters. (3) Kernel-Agnostic MCMC for optimization: A distributionpreserved densification leveraging regularized opacity and a
redefined Beta noise function, together enhancing optimization stability and efficiency independent of kernel shape. 2 RELATED WORK


This section reviews key approaches in novel view synthesis, including implicit NeRFs and explicit 3DGS, highlighting how our
work builds on these advancements and contributes to high-fidelity,
real-time 3D rendering.

2 RELATED WORK


This section reviews key approaches in novel view synthesis, including implicit NeRFs and explicit 3DGS, highlighting how our
work builds on these advancements and contributes to high-fidelity,
real-time 3D rendering. 2.1 Neural Radiance Fields


The introduction of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) [Mildenhall
et al. 2021] revolutionized 3D scene representation and novel view
synthesis. By encoding a continuous volumetric scene within a
multilayer perceptron (MLP), NeRFs jointly learn scene density and
view-dependent color, enabling photorealistic novel view synthesis
through differentiable volumetric rendering. Since their inception, NeRFs have spurred extensive research to
address challenges in convergence speed, computational efficiency,
and scalability. Early advancements, such as FastNeRF [Garbin et al. 2021] and PlenOctrees [Yu et al. 2021], improved efficiency through
caching strategies and spatial acceleration structures. Methods like
NeRF++[Zhang et al. 2020] and DeRF[Rebain et al. 2021] introduced
optimized scene decompositions and novel optimization techniques,
further accelerating training and inference. Additionally, techniques
such as TensoRF [Chen et al. 2022] and DVGO [Sun et al. 2022]
leveraged tensor factorization and voxel grids to reduce memory
requirements and computation time. To address scalability, methods
like Mip-NeRF 360 [Barron et al. 2021], Block-NeRF [Tancik et al. 2022], and UrbanNeRF [Rematas et al.

refractive effects, advancing realism and robustness. Additional
advancements, such as Instant-NGP [Müller et al. 2022] and ZipNeRF [Barron et al. 2023], accelerated NeRF training by introducing a
multi-resolution hash encoding and addressed aliasing issues inherent in grid-based models by incorporating anti-aliasing techniques,
continuously pushing the boundaries of efficiency and quality in
neural scene representation. High-fidelity NeRF rendering requires dense ray sampling and
extensive network evaluations, hindering real-time deployment. Its
implicit scene representation also complicates integration with game
engines and industrial pipelines, which prefer explicit geometry. These challenges drive the exploration of compact representations,
explicit models, and novel optimization techniques to enable interactive, practical applications. 2.2 3D Gaussian Splatting

These challenges drive the exploration of compact representations,

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [Kerbl et al. 2023] offers a compelling alternative to NeRF by representing scenes as collections of
anisotropic Gaussian ellipsoids that capture local properties such
as position, density, and view-dependent appearance. Combining
point-based rendering[Zwicker et al. 2001] with modern machine
learning strategy, it enables flexible and efficient scene representation. However, despite its computational efficiency, 3DGS lags
behind NeRF in photorealism, struggling with fine details, aliasing
artifacts, and complex view-dependent effects. Research has addressed these shortcomings across several fronts. Anti-aliasing methods such as Mip-Splatting [Yu et al. 2023], multiscale approaches [Yan et al. 2024], analytic approximations [Liang
et al. 2024], and scale-adaptive filtering [Song et al. 2024] have been
proposed to reduce jagged edges and shimmering, thereby smoothing the rendered output. Deblurring techniques have also been
explored to enhance clarity. Methods leveraging small MLPs [Lee
et al. 2024], event camera data [Peng et al. 2024], joint optimization of Gaussian parameters with camera trajectory recovery [Oh
et al. 2024; Seiskari et al. 2024; Zhao et al. 2024] have improved the
sharpness of reconstructions from blurred inputs.

integrate motion models and depth-aware filters into the 3DGS

et al. 2023], RadSplat [Niemeyer et al. 2024], Pixel-GS [Zhang et al. 2024], and AtomGS [Liu et al. 2024] focus on efficient Gaussian
placement and density control. Notably, 3DGS-MCMC [Kheradmand
et al. 2024] introduces stochastic processes to refine the sampling
and placement of Gaussians, enhancing both rendering quality and
speed. While these strategies effectively capture scene details and
balance rendering quality with computational cost, they are tailored
specifically to Gaussian kernels.

The primary bottleneck in Gaussian Splatting–based approaches lies
in their reliance on a fixed, smooth splatting kernel and low-order
SH encoding, which inherently hampers their ability to capture flat
surfaces and specular highlights. To overcome this limitation, we
first derive a deformable Beta Kernel function. We then illustrate
how this flexible kernel can be applied to both geometric splatting
and color encoding, enabling the modeling of varying geometric
complexities and lighting frequencies, which enhances the overall
scene representation. Finally, we address the unique challenges
introduced by employing a deformable kernel and detail how our
optimization strategy effectively manages these issues. 4 - Rong Liu, Dylan Sun, Meida Chen, Yue Wang, and Andrew Feng

linearly with the number of reflection lobes and making it more

to radiance discontinuities when view and reflection directions are
orthogonal—the Beta Kernel is inherently bounded. Its input range
is confined to [0 _,_ 1], ensuring that radiance naturally drops to zero
when _𝑅_ [ˆ] _𝑚_ - _𝑉_ [ˆ] = 0. This eliminates artifacts associated with cutoff
truncation and maintains continuity in radiance. Figure 3 illustrates the specular highlights and corresponding

Figure 3 illustrates the specular highlights and corresponding
reflection lobes for different _𝑏𝑚_ values, demonstrating the capability
of Spherical Beta to model both high and low frequency specularities. By integrating bounded support and adaptive shininess, Spherical
Beta enhances the ability to model complex lighting interactions
and specular effects with fewer parameters, thereby improving both
visual fidelity and computational efficiency. 3.4 Kernel-Agnostic Markov Chain Monte Carlo


One of the key innovations of 3DGS is its optimization with densification strategy, which utilizes heuristic gradient thresholds to clone,
split, and prune primitives. Additionally, 3DGS-MCMC redefines
Gaussian Splatting optimization as a Markov Chain Monte Carlo
(MCMC) process by treating each primitive’s opacity as a probability. This approach identifies "dead" primitives—those with opacity
below a pruning threshold—and respawns them by relocating to live
Gaussians through multinomial sampling based on their opacity values. By adjusting both opacity and scale, this method preserves the
underlying probability distribution during densification, thereby
stabilizing the process. Moreover, the introduction of positional
noise encourages exploration and prevents overfitting. However, these heuristic strategies and scale adjustments are
inherently tied to the properties of the Gaussian function, making
them difficult to directly apply to arbitrary kernels.

_Implementations._ Our implementation builds upon the 3DGSMCMC framework [Kheradmand et al. 2024], incorporating modifications to the GSplat library [Ye et al. 2024b]. Specifically, we
integrate the Beta Kernel and Spherical Beta (SB) functions, which
are fully explicit and differentiable, implemented in CUDA for optimized performance. By default, we utilize two light sources in
Spherical Beta component per primitive (i.e., _𝑠𝑏_ = 2), unless otherwise specified. To ensure that the Beta Kernel initially resembles the
Gaussian Kernel, we set _𝑏_ to zero at initialization.

By default, we utilize two light sources in
Spherical Beta component per primitive (i.e., _𝑠𝑏_ = 2), unless otherwise specified. To ensure that the Beta Kernel initially resembles the
Gaussian Kernel, we set _𝑏_ to zero at initialization. We observe that
different scenes exhibit varying convergence speeds when training the model for the default 30,000 iterations. To accommodate
these variations, we have integrated a flexible stopping strategy
with patience of 10k iterations into the framework, allowing for two
training modes: (Ours, 30K) and (Ours, Full). Detailed training times
and iteration counts for each scene are provided in Appendix B. For
additional hyperparameters and configuration settings, please refer
to Appendix F. 4.2 Results and Comparisons


_Radiance Field Reconstruction._ We evaluate DBS using the standard 3DGS evaluation pipeline across several widely recognized
datasets, including Mip-NeRF 360 [Barron et al. 2021], Tanks and
Temples [Knapitsch et al. 2017], Deep Blending [Hedman et al. 2018],
and the NeRF Synthetic dataset [Mildenhall et al. 2021]. Performance
is measured using standard metrics: Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio
(PSNR), Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM), and Learned
Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS). For the Mip-NeRF 360,
Tanks and Temples, and Deep Blending datasets, we utilize the
Colmap Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point cloud provided by the
3DGS [Kerbl et al. 2023] repository for initialization.

Ablation Studies on Tank&Temples and Deep Blending datasets. _Ablation Study._ Table 3 compares PSNR and memory usage on
the Tanks & Temples and Deep Blending datasets across several
DBS configurations: moving from 3DGS-MCMC to a DBS-MCMC
raises PSNR from 24.29 dB to 24.45 dB (Tanks & Temples) and from
29.67 dB to 29.88 dB (Deep Blending); switching to Kernel-Agnostic
MCMC further boosts PSNR to 24.57 dB and 30.03 dB with no added
memory; varying the number of spherical-beta light sources (sb)
reveals a trade-off: sb = 1 uses only 155.8 MB but yields 24.53 dB/30.04
dB, sb = 2 hits a sweet spot at 200.3 MB for 24.79 dB/30.10 dB, while



sb = 4 or 6 slightly increase PSNR (up to 24.81 dB/30.12 dB) at much
higher memory (289–378 MB); finally, adding our flexible stopping
strategy to the sb = 2 setup (“DBS (full)”) delivers a final bump to
24.85 dB and 30.12 dB. 4.3 Beta Decomposition


Leveraging the deformable nature of the Beta Kernel, our framework
enables decomposition of both geometry and lighting post-training. This capability arises from the dual role of the Beta Kernel in encoding volumetric splatting and view-dependent color information. _Geometry Decomposition._ The Beta Kernel’s parameter _𝑏_ intrinsically controls the geometry frequency representation of each primitive. Lower _𝑏_ values correspond to lower-frequency primitives,
which predominantly capture the fundamental geometric structures of the scene.

( University of Southern California )

chunks.chunk_section: Deformable Beta Splatting
chunks.text:
[Deformable Beta Splatting] - Deformable Beta Splatting

_Geometry Decomposition._ The Beta Kernel’s parameter _𝑏_ intrinsically controls the geometry frequency representation of each primitive. Lower _𝑏_ values correspond to lower-frequency primitives,
which predominantly capture the fundamental geometric structures of the scene. Conversely, higher _𝑏_ values encapsulate higherfrequency details, such as textures and fine surface variations. By setting a mask based on the _𝑏_ parameter, we can selectively
isolate primitives based on their frequency contributions. We can
also do a simple binary split based on a threshold ( _e.g_ . the mean of _𝑏_
values across all primitives). Primitives with _𝑏_ below the threshold
primarily represent the scene’s solid geometry, with primitives of _𝑏_
above the threshold provides high-frequency texture details. Figure 4 illustrates how Beta Kernels separate geometry from texture on real-world datasets. In the "treehill" scene, the bark texture
is represented using primitives with beta parameter _𝑏_ . Similarly, in
the "garden" scene, detailed textures on the tabletop are removed,
preserving the overall table geometry. _Lighting Decomposition._ Since Beta Splatting integrates a learnable Phong Reflection Model [Phong 1975], we can extract diffuse
component through taking only the base color _𝑐_ 0. Conversely, only
enabling specular component gives the view-dependent specular
lighting effects.

_Lighting Decomposition._ Since Beta Splatting integrates a learnable Phong Reflection Model [Phong 1975], we can extract diffuse
component through taking only the base color _𝑐_ 0. Conversely, only
enabling specular component gives the view-dependent specular
lighting effects. For comparison, we only enable zero degree of SH
for diffuse color while non zero degree for specular effects. The results in Figure 6 illustrate the effectiveness of this approach. In the "bicycle" scene, the black bench is separated from the white
highlights, a result unattainable with Gaussian Splatting. Similarly,
in the "bonsai" scene, Beta Splatting successfully reconstructs the
bright highlight component of the bonsai container, while Gaussian
Splatting fails to capture such extreme view-dependent details. 10 - Rong Liu, Dylan Sun, Meida Chen, Yue Wang, and Andrew Feng


5 CONCLUSION


We presented Deformable Beta Splatting (DBS), a novel approach
that advances real-time radiance field rendering through three key
innovations: Deformable Beta Kernels for adaptive geometry representation, Spherical Betas for efficient view-dependent color encoding, and Kernel-Agnostic MCMC that enhances optimization
stability and efficiency by relying solely on regularized opacity. These innovations allow DBS to achieve superior visual quality
with less memory and computing resources than prior methods.

These innovations allow DBS to achieve superior visual quality
with less memory and computing resources than prior methods. _Limitations._ As our framework is rasterization-based, it occasionally produces popping artifacts due to depth approximation
inaccuracies during the sorting process. While adaptive, Spherical Beta Functions struggle to model mirror-like reflections and
anisotropic specular highlights effectively. In addition, the frustum
model causes Beta Kernels to optimize flat geometries for distant
backgrounds, which impacts the overall beta geometry distribution. These limitations offer opportunities for further refinement and
enhancement of the framework. ACKNOWLEDGMENTS

B PER-SCENE RESULTS


Our per-scene evaluation on the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset shows that,
on diffuse scenes ( _e.g_ ., “bicycle,” “stump,” and “flowers”), Deformable
Beta Splatting achieves the comparable performance of prior works,
while on scenes with strong specular reflections ( _e.g_ ., “counter”),
it surpasses 3DGS-MCMC and Zip-NeRF by over 1 dB in PSNR. This gain demonstrates the ability of DBS to faithfully reconstruct
intricate specular lighting in challenging scenarios. C KERNEL COMPARISON



In addition to Table 3, we isolate the effect of the splatting kernel
through an ablation study, disabling all view-dependent color terms
(sh=0, sb=0) and comparing the standard Gaussian kernel (3DGS)
to our deformable Beta kernel (DBS). Both models are trained on
the Mip-NeRF 360 training set and evaluated on test views under
MCMC densification schedules. Fig. 7. Reconstruction quality on the Mip-NeRF 360 without viewdependent color-encodings. Deformable Beta Splatting (DBS) consistently
outperforms 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), confirming the stronger representation ability of the Beta kernel. 14 - Rong Liu, Dylan Sun, Meida Chen, Yue Wang, and Andrew Feng


Figure 7 plots PSNR (left axis) and MSE (right axis) as a function of
the total number of primitives. Although both kernels improve with
more primitives, the Gaussian baseline plateaus around 1.5 M, while
the Beta kernel continues to yield gains.

D.2 Validity of the Small Opacity Assumption


A natural question arises regarding the role of the small opacity
prior used in our framework. At first glance, encouraging primitives to remain semi-transparent may appear counterintuitive: in
surface-based representations, higher opacity is typically desirable to achieve clean geometry. However, our approach lies in
Volumetric Density field. Volumetric methods—such as NeRF and
3DGS—fundamentally differ from surface-based techniques. In a
volumetric framework, each primitive contributes only a small opacity, and the final image emerges from the accumulation of many
low-opacity contributions.

Volumetric methods—such as NeRF and
3DGS—fundamentally differ from surface-based techniques. In a
volumetric framework, each primitive contributes only a small opacity, and the final image emerges from the accumulation of many
low-opacity contributions. Within this paradigm, enforcing high perprimitive opacity can improve geometric fidelity and facilitate mesh
extraction, but contradicts the core assumptions of smooth transmittance accumulation and degrades visual quality. Notable examples of
this trade-off include NeuS [Wang et al. 2021] vs NeRF [Mildenhall
et al. 2021] and SuGaR [Guédon and Lepetit 2023] vs 3DGS [Kerbl
et al. 2023]. In contrast, applying a moderate opacity prior aligns
with the volumetric principle, supports distribution-preserving densification, and further stabilizes the optimization process. To quantify the impact of the opacity regularization, we analyze
its effect both theoretically and empirically. In Figure 8, we visualize
the original distribution (blue) and its densified distribution (red) as
defined in Equation (33), across different kernel shapes. As opacity
decreases, the discrepancy between the two distributions diminishes,
with near-perfect alignment observed when the opacity approaches
0.1. This behavior supports our theoretical analysis: under the smallopacity regime, the densified distribution accurately preserves the
original, regardless of the number of clones or the kernel function
used.

After training, we apply a
post-training compression pipeline adapted from [Morgenstern et al. 2025] to further reduce each model’s on-disk footprint. Specifically,
we firstly sort and reorder the parameters so that similar values are
adjacent, maximizing the efficiency of lossless PNG compression. Next, we quantize most parameters from 32-bit floats down to 8-bit,
allowing us to save them into PNG images. However, because we
observed that reducing the precision of the 3D position to 8 bits
causes a severe degradation in rendering quality, we preserve those
values at full 32-bit precision, distributing them across four separate
images, while all other parameters are stored as 8-bit PNGs. We conduct these experiments on the Mip-360 dataset and report
mean metrics across nine scenes in Table 7. As the model is pruned
from 3.11 M primitives (DBS-full) to 1 M (DBS-1M) and then to
0.49 M (DBS-490K), we observe a graceful degradation in rendering
fidelity: mean PSNR decreases from 28.75 dB to 28.42 dB to 28.03
dB, SSIM from 0.845 to 0.831 to 0.816, and LPIPS increases from
0.179 to 0.205 to 0.232. In parallel, the raw on-disk footprint contracts substantially—from 356 MB (2.11x relative to vanilla 3DGS) to
114 MB (6.58x) to 56 MB (13.42x). Applying uniform post-training



PNG compression further amplifies these storage savings by approximately 5x–6x: final sizes become 63 MB, 22 MB, and 11 MB,
corresponding to overall compression ratios of 11.9x, 33.7x, and
66.2x relative to 3DGS.

Title: Designing 3D Anisotropic Frame Fields with Odeco Tensors

Authors: Haikuan Zhu, 
Hongbo Li 
( Wayne State University ), Hsueh-Ti Derek Liu ( Roblox and University of British Columbia ), Wenping Wang ( Texas A&M University ),  
Jing Hua, Zichun Zhong ( Wayne State University )

Abstract: Abstract: This paper introduces a method to synthesize a 3D tensor field within a constrained geometric domain represented as a tetrahedral mesh. Whereas previous techniques optimize for isotropic fields, we focus on anisotropic tensor fields that are smooth and aligned with the domain boundary or user guidance. The key ingredient of our method is a novel computational design framework, built on top of the symmetric orthogonally decomposable (odeco) tensor representation, to optimize the stretching ratios and orientations for each tensor in the domain. In contrast to past techniques designed only for isotropic tensors, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in generating smooth volumetric tensor fields with high anisotropy and shape conformity, especially for the domain with complex shapes. We apply these anisotropic tensor fields to various applications, such as anisotropic meshing, structural mechanics, and fabrication.

[HAIKUAN ZHU, Wayne State University, USA](HTTPS://ORCID.ORG/0000-0001-5740-0599)
[HONGBO LI, Wayne State University, USA](HTTPS://ORCID.ORG/0009-0005-9072-1489)

This paper introduces a method to synthesize a 3D tensor field within a

constrained geometric domain represented as a tetrahedral mesh. Whereas

previous techniques optimize for _isotropic_ fields, we focus on _anisotropic_

tensor fields that are smooth and aligned with the domain boundary or user

[Designing 3D Anisotropic Frame Fields with Odeco Tensors] - Designing 3D Anisotropic Frame Fields with Odeco Tensors

[HAIKUAN ZHU, Wayne State University, USA](HTTPS://ORCID.ORG/0000-0001-5740-0599)
[HONGBO LI, Wayne State University, USA](HTTPS://ORCID.ORG/0009-0005-9072-1489)
[HSUEH-TI DEREK LIU, Roblox & University of British Columbia, Canada](HTTPS://ORCID.ORG/0009-0001-1753-4485)
[WENPING WANG, Texas A&M University, USA](HTTPS://ORCID.ORG/0000-0002-2284-3952)
[JING HUA, Wayne State University, USA](HTTPS://ORCID.ORG/0000-0002-3981-2933)
[ZICHUN ZHONG](HTTPS://ORCID.ORG/0000-0001-6489-6502) [∗], Wayne State University, USA



This paper introduces a method to synthesize a 3D tensor field within a

constrained geometric domain represented as a tetrahedral mesh. Whereas

previous techniques optimize for _isotropic_ fields, we focus on _anisotropic_

tensor fields that are smooth and aligned with the domain boundary or user

guidance. The key ingredient of our method is a novel computational design

framework, built on top of the _symmetric orthogonally decomposable_ (odeco)

tensor representation, to optimize the stretching ratios and orientations for

each tensor in the domain. In contrast to past techniques designed only for

_isotropic_ tensors, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in generating
smooth volumetric tensor fields with high _anisotropy_ and shape conformity,

especially for the domain with complex shapes. We apply these anisotropic

tensor fields to various applications, such as anisotropic meshing, structural

mechanics, and fabrication.

1 INTRODUCTION


Directional fields plays a central role in numerous graphics and en
gineering applications, ranging from texturing [Ma et al. 2011], de
formation [Von Funck et al. 2006], to meshing [Li et al. 2024; Zhong

et al. 2018]. Although such a tensor field is relatively well-studied

on _surfaces_ [Vaxman et al. 2016], computing _volumetric_ tensor fields

receives far less attention, despite its importance. Previous attempts,

such as [Corman and Crane 2019; Palmer et al. 2020; Ray et al. 2016], propose techniques for computing volumetric tensor fields

and demonstrate applications in e.g., hexahedral meshing. How
ever, their formulations solely focus on _isotropic_ tensors, and fail to
generate practical _anisotropic_ fields.

Overall,

our main contributions are:


  - We introduce a method for optimizing volumetric tensor fields
with a novel focus on _anisotropy_ . - Our optimization framework results in a smooth volumetric

tensor field with high conformity to surface normals and

curvatures, supported by our theoretical analysis. - Our method incorporates user controls, demonstrating appli
cations in anisotropic meshing, microstructure fabrication,

and material design. 2 RELATED WORK


In this section, we review the related literature on cross and frame

field, as well as 3D tensor field. 2.1 Cross and Frame Field


In geometric modeling and processing, there are lots of work in

the design of direction fields in 2D and 3D domains, such as cross

fields and their applications in quad meshing [Vaxman et al. 2016]. Methods to compute smooth cross fields on the surface with align

feature alignment when smoothing the target direction fields. One

of the most prominent representations is the trigonometric pair,

The main geometric application for 3D frame

fields is hexahedral and hex-dominant mesh generation [Gao et al. 2017; Li et al. 2012; Liu et al. 2018; Lyon et al. 2016; Nieser et al. 2011;

Sokolov et al. 2016]. [Huang et al. 2011] introduces a particularly

convenient representation of a 3D octahedral frame as a rotation of

the spherical function (SH). ACM Trans. Graph., Vol. 44, No. 4, Article 0. Publication date: August 2025. Inspired by the method of [Huang et al. 2011], [Ray et al. 2016]

produces a smooth 3D frame field, which varies smoothly inside the

volume, and matches the normals of the volume boundary. [Solomon

et al. 2017] leverages the boundary element method (BEM) to achieve

infinite resolution within the volume, enabling the continuous as
signment of frames to points in the interior based solely on a triangle

mesh discretization of the boundary. [Corman and Crane 2019] pro
poses an alternative method based on Cartan’s method of moving

frames for computing a frame field with a prescribed singularity

structure, utilizing a discretized connection on a frame bundle. [Fang

et al. 2021] generates a smooth frame field for a Riemannian metric

field that is flat away from singularities under a few intuitive con
straints. But these representations of 3D cross and frame fields only

consider the orientations. 2.2 3D Tensor Field


Traditional cross and frame fields describe only orientations or direc
tions within space.

But these representations of 3D cross and frame fields only

consider the orientations. 2.2 3D Tensor Field


Traditional cross and frame fields describe only orientations or direc
tions within space. Research on those direction fields is unable nat
urally extend to the processing of tensor fields. This is because a 3D

tensor contains not only directional information but also anisotropic

scaling information (stretching ratios). 3D tensor fields have been

widely used in different domains for decades, such as anisotropic

meshing [Loseille 2014; Yamakawa and Shimada 2000; Zhong et al. 2018], microstructure design [Martínez et al. 2018; Wu et al. 2019],

deformation [Zheng and Pang 2002], simulation [Dick et al. 2009],

visualization [Bi et al. 2019; Hung et al. 2023], and mechanics [Hergl

et al. 2021; Kratz et al. 2014]. However, computing and designing

volumetric tensor fields has been little studied. Although [Palacios

et al. 2016] provides a tensor field design framework that specializes

in the topology and singularities, the way of element-wise smooth
ing of the tensor matrix always leads to unsatisfying transitions. Besides, their normal alignment is achieved by tensor modification

by force. Recently, benefiting from the symmetric orthogonally de
composable (odeco) tensor varieties introduced in [Boralevi et al. 2017; Robeva 2016], it allows for an exact one-to-one correspon
dence between symmetric tensors and homogeneous polynomials.

Recently, benefiting from the symmetric orthogonally de
composable (odeco) tensor varieties introduced in [Boralevi et al. 2017; Robeva 2016], it allows for an exact one-to-one correspon
dence between symmetric tensors and homogeneous polynomials. This property enables us to decompose a tensor into its orientation

and the stretching components. [Palmer et al. 2020] is the first to

use anisotropic tensors to have energetically cheap singular curves;

however, their limited investigation of anisotropy results in a simple

smoothed odeco tensor field with near uniform stretching ratios. Moreover, as observed in our experiments, the projection which is

required in their method becomes unstable when flexible stretching

ratios are introduced. Recently, [Couplet et al. 2024] proposes inte
grable frame fields using odeco representation in both isotropic and

anisotropic settings; however, they only focus on 2D planar frame

field design. Extending their approach to 3D volumetric settings

remains an open challenge. In this work, we address the challenging

problem of designing 3D anisotropic odeco tensor fields in volume

with the consideration of large stretching ratios in the company of

additional boundary characteristics. 3 ODECO TENSOR REPRESENTATION

mesh Ω = (V _,_ T) with vertices V and tetrahedra T . The boundary

An odeco tensor can be equivalently represented by either an odeco

matrix or an odeco polynomial. Thus, we visualize the odeco tensor

by either an odeco polynomial (e.g., Fig. 2) or the cuboid-style (e.g.,

Fig. 9) or ellipsoid-style glyph (e.g., Fig. 10) that is created by the

corresponding eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Eigenvalues and eigen
vectors are obtained by singular value decomposition (SVD) of the

tensor matrix. The volumetric odeco tensor field is also visualized

by the integral curves (e.g., Fig. 1). These integral curves are initially

randomly sampled and traced along the eigenvector of the largest

eigenvalue. 3.5 Comparison Against Baselines


Our odeco tensor representation [Robeva 2016] shares similarities

with previous methods for computing _isotropic_ tensor fields, such

as [Palmer et al. 2020; Zhang et al. 2020]. In this work, we adopt

the same odeco tensor representation that is first used by Palmer

et al. [2020].

minimum. As this warm start computation only happens on the

result is aware of the “rough” anisotropy from **𝚲** _𝑤𝑎𝑟𝑚_ . However,

such a coordinate descent solver may struggle to converge to good

solutions (e.g., [Bouaziz et al. 2014]). We experience the same issue

if we merely use a coordinate descent solver back and forth between

**𝚲** _,_ **𝚯** . We thus merely use this as a tool as a fast warm start on the

orientations, and still solve **𝚲** _,_ **𝚯** jointly for a better convergence.

natural choice for achieving exact feature alignment is to enforce

the major lobes fixed along the sharp feature edges, as we have done

for the normal alignment. For corner points which typically are

singularities, we arbitrarily assign one of its feature edge directions

since their stretching ratios will be further optimized.

6.1 Implementation Details


We implement and evaluate our algorithms on a PC with a 3.6GHz

Core CPU, 32GB RAM, and Windows 11. We test our algorithms on

various 3D models from the Thingi10k dataset [Zhou et al. 2016],

with varying resolutions, complicated geometry, and challenging

sharp or weak features. The input tetrahedral meshes are generated

by TetGen [Hang 2015] from the surface meshes. We list the detailed

In this work, we are able to handle different kinds of user’s de
sign guidance in the input for our 3D tensor design. The detailed

description is given as follows:

ratios at the region of interest in the volume domain as the

design guidance are processed by the Blender software, such

as Figs. 4, 7, 17. - Tensor-based guidance: User-specified tensors (both stretch
ing ratios and orientations) at the region of interest in the

volume domain as constraints are designed by the interactive

tensor design framework in [Palacios et al. 2016], such as

Figs. 1, 10, 17. The specified tensors can be either degener
ate or non-degenerate, distributed at specific points or along

curves. More details are introduced in [Palacios et al.

6.4 Evaluations and Comparisons


Fig. 8 demonstrates a gallery of our optimal shape-conforming AOTF

results. It validates our method on challenging models with complex

shape variations and features from the Thingi10k dataset [Zhou et al. 2016]. For each model, the only input is the boundary anisotropy

guidance coming from the curvature magnitudes (stretching ratios),

and the normal alignment and strict feature alignment are automat
ically applied. The depicted integral curves are initially sampled

and traced along the major lobes of tensors. These integral curves

effectively align with the local geometry, while maintaining the

smoothness with the automatic balance in regions with intricate

details and features. In the following, we compare our method with

the state-of-the-art in volumetric tensor designs by using odeco

representation [Palmer et al. 2020] and symmetric matrix represen
tation [Palacios et al. 2016]. In Fig. 9, we compare with [Palmer et al. 2020] in shape
conforming tensor field designs for complicated 3D models. The

common constraints are normal alignments in both methods. We

have the same smoothness energy form using odeco _𝐸𝑠_ with the

method of [Palmer et al. 2020]. The results of [Palmer et al. 2020]

are implemented by their source code. We apply boundary curva
ture tensor (both magnitudes and directions) as hard constraints

in their mMBO-based method in [Palmer et al. 2020].

In Fig. 10, we compare with [Palacios et al. 2016] and [Palmer et al. 2020] in smooth tensor field designs from user-specified constraints. To make a fair comparison, we only apply normal alignment and

user-specified interior constraints, which are used by all methods. The results of [Palacios et al. 2016] are obtained from their developed

framework. The results of [Palmer et al. 2020] are implemented by

their source code. Both [Palacios et al. 2016] and [Palmer et al. 2020]

have limited freedom on the boundary, which curbs the boundary

odeco tensors. A fundamental reason for the artifacts in [Palacios


et al. 2016] is the way of computational operations on tensor matrix

element. [Palmer et al. 2020] improves the smoothness but still

shows a weaker transition near the boundary. The main reason is

their un-normalized basis when denoting by a lower-dimensional

vector, as well as the projection operation that limits the flexibility

of stretching ratios. However, our method outperforms both of

them in terms of the lower smoothness energy. Visually, our results

achieve a much smoother transition between the user-specified hard

constraints and the normal-aligned boundary tensors. In addition,

we demonstrate the corresponding singularity graphs in Fig. 11.

we demonstrate the corresponding singularity graphs in Fig. 11. 7 APPLICATIONS


In addition to the evaluations in the previous section, we intro
duce some downstream applications of our proposed AOTFs on

anisotropic surface and volume meshing, fabrication of anisotropic

microstructures, and elastic material designs. 7.1 Anisotropic Surface and Volume Meshing


Anisotropic meshes have great importance in shape approximations

and numerical methods to solve partial differential equations. The

anisotropic meshes outperform isotropic meshes in scenarios where

directional features or variations in the geometry need to be cap
tured effectively. They improve the accuracy of the solution and

decrease the computational cost [Alliez et al. 2003; Huang 2005;

Narain et al. 2012]. The result quality of the current anisotropic

meshing methods mainly depend on the input tensor fields [Zhong

et al. 2018]. Our optimal AOTFs offer good quality meshing results

with high fidelity and smoothness, primarily because the stretching

ratios are preserved rather than smoothed while the orientations

are automatically optimized and smoothed, as observed from the

comparison with field smoothing in Fig. 12. In Fig. 12, we demonstrate the performance of our optimal AOTFs

on the anisotropic surface and volume meshing.

on the anisotropic surface and volume meshing. To demonstrate

the strength of our shape conformity in our tensor field design, we

compare the anisotropic meshes with the curvature tensor fields

and our optimal AOTFs. The anisotropic triangular meshing is im
plemented by the state-of-the-art feature-sensitive anisotropic tri
angular meshing method in [Li et al. 2024], which is capable of

keeping weak features. We use the same number of vertices in the

output anisotropic meshes for comparison. We compute the Haus
dorff distance _𝐷ℎ_ between the dense input mesh and the generated

anisotropic mesh to measure the ability to express complex local geo
metric variations of the given shapes. Compared with the estimated

raw curvature tensor field (obtained as discussed in Section 6.2) as

input, our optimal AOTFs offer higher fidelity and smoother mesh
ing results. Compared with the post-smoothed curvature tensor

field by Laplacian smoothing used in [Palacios et al. 2016], although

their smoothness is improved, the original curvature stretching

ratios and boundary geometric features are not well maintained. Furthermore, over-smoothed tensor fields with smaller _𝐸𝑠_ in Fig. 12

(b) may cause a worse fidelity with a larger Hausdorff distance _𝐷ℎ_ .

Furthermore, we further demonstrate our applications on

anisotropic tetrahedral meshing. For instance, we apply our op
timal volumetric AOTFs to [Zhong et al. 2018]. Fig. 13 shows that

our AOTFs take user-specified tensors as constraints and curva
ture magnitudes as guidance to obtain the tetrahedral meshes with

both shape conformity and user-desired orientations and stretch
ing ratios. Since current anisotropic tetrahedral meshing methods

completely depend on the guidance of the input tensor metrics, our

method provides a promising and high-quality input for them. Note

that, the singularity graphs may look complex since we try to keep

the large stretching ratios on the boundary. However, due to the

unstructured nature of tetrahedral meshing, the singularity graphs

do not affect the mesh quality.

do not affect the mesh quality. 7.2 Fabrication of Anisotropic Microstructures


Recent advancements in the design of volumetric anisotropic

microstructures, such as stress-aligned anisotropic truss struc
ture [Arora et al. 2019], anisotropic elastic microstructures [Martínez

et al. 2018; Martínez et al. 2017] and orientable structures with

anisotropy [Tricard et al. 2020], rely on tensor fields as input to

enable the creation of anisotropic behaviors. Previous tensor design

methods introduce anisotropy by requiring both user-specified ori
entations and stretching ratios as input, which demands extensive

manual design effort for complex shapes. In contrast, our method

automatically optimizes the orientations while only referring to

the specified stretching ratios. As a result, the optimized AOTFs

naturally conform to surface curvatures and preserve geometric

features, leading to improved boundary layers in the generated

microstructures. _Tensor Field Smoothing_ . Numerically simulated tensor fields, such

as stress-simulated and fluid-simulated, are usually extremely noisy

and lack shape conformity. Thus, our method shows the capability

of not only increasing the overall smoothness but also balancing the

fidelity with the inputs. Similar to Eq.

be considered as AOTFs since they involve three orthogonal direc

Motivated by the

demand for artificial soft hands in robotics, our method streamlines

the design process by requiring the magnitudes of Young’s moduli

as input. By default, the orientations of the optimized Young’s mod
uli align with the boundary shape, simplifying design operations in

most cases. Additionally, we introduce orientation constraints used

for joint designs (e.g., to bend the fingers). The optimal Young’s

moduli automatically balance the shape conformity (especially for

fingers) and user-specified constraints (for joints). After obtain
ing the optimal Young’s modulus field, the tensors are normalized

and projected onto the material space depicted in Fig. 16. The fi
nal material is then modeled and fabricated based on the retrieved

microstructure parameters. The generated microstructures nicely

satisfy user’s design requirement as shown in Fig. 17. 8 CONCLUSION


In this paper, we develop a new computational paradigm, AOTF,

for generating complicated anisotropic tensor fields in volume. To

our knowledge, this is the first odeco tensor method capable of

designing smooth anisotropic tensor fields with several nice proper
ties – naturally aligning with the domain boundary and geometric

features, as well as providing users with the flexibility of anisotropy

Graph., Vol. 44, No. 4, Article 0. Publication date: August 2025. control where needed. Our method demonstrates promising poten
tial in terms of anisotropic meshing, microstructure fabrication, and

material design. 9 LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK


The proposed AOTF computation is a highly nonconvex problem,

which could be difficult to solve because it is possible to get stuck in

a local minimum. In this work, we propose a warm start-based joint

optimization of tensor orientations and stretching ratios, which

leads to a much faster convergence to a better local minimum, but

it cannot guarantee to reach a theoretical global minimal solution. From our observations, while our AOTF results usually contain sin
gularities with higher smoothness energy, during the optimization

we mitigate these high energy regions associated with the singu
larities by optimizing both orientations and stretching ratios. This

can relieve singularity issues. However, we have not considered the

topology and structure of singularities in our tensor field design

framework, which is beyond the scope of this work. In the future,

we will improve the computational speed by using GPU-based or

deep learning-based algorithm and implementation. Since 3D tensor-induced designs are essential for enhancing ac
curacy, efficiency, and stability in simulations across various fields,

we will apply our method in quad or hex meshing, deformation,

and texturing, etc.

chunks.text:
[Designing 3D Anisotropic Frame Fields with Odeco Tensors] - Designing 3D Anisotropic Frame Fields with Odeco Tensors

Since 3D tensor-induced designs are essential for enhancing ac
curacy, efficiency, and stability in simulations across various fields,

we will apply our method in quad or hex meshing, deformation,

and texturing, etc. Especially, 3D anisotropic frame fields play a

critical role in anisotropic hex meshing. However, to the best of our

knowledge, there exists no tool that can generate anisotropic hex

meshes from a tensor field, especially with large stretching ratios. The primary difficulty lies in ensuring that the odeco tensor field

produces a singular graph that is meshable or integrable. Promis
ingly, the 2D planar results from [Couplet et al. 2024] indicate that

anisotropy significantly improves integrability, suggesting that a ro
bust method for hex meshing could become feasible when extended

to anisotropic cases. Therefore, our work on anisotropic frame field

design and optimization strategies could serve as a good start to

inspire future work on anisotropic hex meshing. ACKNOWLEDGMENTS

Title: Differentiable Geometric Acoustic Path Tracing using Time-Resolved Path Replay Backpropagation

Authors: Ugo Finnendahl , Markus Worchel , 
Tobias Juterbock, 
Daniel Wujecki, 
Fabian Brinkmann, 
Stefan Weinzierl, Marc Alexa ( TU Berlin )

Abstract: Abstract Differentiable rendering has become a key ingredient in solving challenging inverse problems in computer graphics and vision. Existing systems can simulate and differentiate the spatial propagation of light.
We exploit the duality of light transport simulations and geometric acoustics to apply differential rendering techniques to established acoustic simulation methods.
The resulting system is capable of simulating sound according to the geometrical acoustics model and computing derivatives of the output energy spectrograms with respect to arbitrary parameters of the scene, including materials, emitters, microphones, and scene geometry. Contrary to current differentiable transient rendering, we can handle arbitrary simulation depths and achieve constant memory and linear execution times by presenting a temporal extension of Path Replay Backpropagation. We verify our model against established simulation software, and demonstrate the capabilities of optimization with gradients at examples of inverse acoustics and optimizing room parameters. This opens up a new field of research for acoustic optimization that could be as impactful for the acoustic community as differentiable rendering was for the graphics community. differentiable rendering, geometrical acoustics, physically-based simulation, acoustic optimization Computing methodologies Ray tracing; Modeling and simulation;

Publication date: August 2025. 2 - Finnendahl and Worchel et al. 1 INTRODUCTION


_Rendering_ commonly refers to the mapping of parameters describing a _scene_, such as geometry, reflectance properties, location and

characteristics of emitters as well as sensors, to the signal at the

sensor. If we summarize the scene parameters as a set of values

_𝝅_, we can express the rendering process as the computation of
the vector-valued function _𝑅_ ( _𝝅_ ). In any application that requires
finding, adjusting, or optimizing _𝝅_ based on requirements or goals

for the rendering output, it has proven extremely useful to know

the Jacobian J _𝑅_ ( _𝝅_ ): As long as the objective can be modeled as a
scalar (and continuously differentiable) _loss_ function L, optimizing
the function L( _𝑅_ ( _𝝅_ )) can be performed with gradient-based meth
ods. The need for gradients of the rendering function, especially

in the context of neural networks in vision tasks, has led to the

development of _differentiable rendering_ . Great progress has been made in differentiable rendering of light

in recent years (Section 2.2), in particular using the method of _path_
_tracing_ [Kajiya 1986; Veach 1998]. In this work, we make use of these

recent techniques to simulate the propagation of sound. Although

differentiable acoustic rendering has recently appeared in the liter
ature [Stanziola et al. 2023; Zhi et al. 2023], to our knowledge, we

present the first fully differentiable acoustic path tracer.

[Differentiable Geometric Acoustic Path Tracing using Time-Resolved Path Replay Backpropagation] - Differentiable Geometric Acoustic Path Tracing using Time-Resolved Path Replay Backpropagation

Although

differentiable acoustic rendering has recently appeared in the liter
ature [Stanziola et al. 2023; Zhi et al. 2023], to our knowledge, we

present the first fully differentiable acoustic path tracer. While both light and sound are waves and exhibit very similar

phenomena, the importance of various aspects in applications is very

different. Some aspects are often ignored in the simulation of both

types, such as nonlinear interactions or variations in propagation

speed. _Diffraction_ or _interference_ is generally more important for the

simulation of sound propagation, because many objects interacting

with audible sound are at the scale of the wavelengths. Nevertheless,

the simulation of sound propagation has many applications even

when ignoring interference and diffraction effects (Section 2.1). The

main difference for the simulation of sound and light is _propagation_

over time. For the simulation of light, we commonly assume instan
taneous propagation. The function _𝑅_ ( _𝝅_ ) is resolved in the angular

domain, but not in time. Conversely, for sound, it is often acceptable

to model omnidirectional receivers without any spatial resolution,

but it is crucial to resolve the time domain. After introducing some background (Section 3), we develop ex
tensions to differentiable path tracing that enable proper handling

of time (Section 4).

[Differentiable Geometric Acoustic Path Tracing using Time-Resolved Path Replay Backpropagation] - Differentiable Geometric Acoustic Path Tracing using Time-Resolved Path Replay Backpropagation

After introducing some background (Section 3), we develop ex
tensions to differentiable path tracing that enable proper handling

of time (Section 4). We adopt a functional perspective, where quan
tities are represented as continuous functions of time, and show

that algorithms from differentiable light transport can be naturally

cast in this framework. In principle, the derivatives of the render
ing function _𝑅_, no matter how complex, can be determined using

automatic differentiation [Jakob et al. 2022b,a; Nimier-David et al. 2019; Zhang et al. 2020]. In practice, however, the problem is difficult

because the complexity of _𝑅_ ( _𝝅_ ) makes tape-based automatic dif
ferentiation infeasible for all but the most simplistic problems. We

propose a time-resolved extension of Path Replay Backpropagation

(PRB) [Vicini et al. 2021], which is essential for efficient differentiable

simulations as derivatives can be computed with constant memory

and linear time. Despite handling (discretized) functions over time,

we show that this time-resolved backpropagation algorithm has

only minimal overhead over its light transport equivalent. ACM Trans. Graph., Vol. 44, No. 4, Article . Publication date: August 2025. We continue by verifying our implementation (Section 5), first

showing that the forward simulation reproduces established simula
tion software based on geometric acoustics.

showing that the forward simulation reproduces established simula
tion software based on geometric acoustics. Then, we demonstrate

that the differentiable simulation not only correctly accounts for the

effect of moving geometry on the time but also that time-resolved

Path Replay Backpropagation efficiently computes derivatives that

are equivalent to tape-based automatic differentiation. We show several applications and inverse acoustics problems

for which gradient-based solutions are enabled by differentiable

acoustic path tracing (Section 6), including the optimization and

recovery of reflectance properties of surfaces or the position of

sound sources and geometry to improve the sound distribution. We conclude by discussing the limitations inherited from the light

transport PRB method and those resulting from ignoring the wave

nature of sound and how they might be overcome (Section 7). 2 RELATED WORK

particular for interaction in virtual environments [Funkhouser et al.

Graphics techniques have been used

in acoustics mostly for improved efficiency of computation, for ex
ample by exploiting GPUs [Mehra et al. 2012; Savioja et al. 2010], in

particular for interaction in virtual environments [Funkhouser et al. 1998; Manocha and Lin 2009; Mehra et al. 2015; Taylor et al. 2009;

Tsingos et al. 2001; Yeh et al. 2013] and precomputation-based meth
ods for fast synthesis as needed in games [Raghuvanshi and Snyder

2014, 2018]. Physically-based simulation has been extended from

generating images of the scene to also generating sounds from the

interaction of objects [James et al. 2006; Wang et al. 2018; Zheng and

James 2010, 2011]. Here, we focus on applications that involve either

inverse problems (such as recovering scene parameters from ob
servations) or optimization (such as improving application specific

properties by adjusting scene parameters). In the following, we briefly review geometric techniques for room

acoustic simulation and how they are currently being extended

towards differentiable sound rendering. Then we provide a brief

summary of differentiable rendering for light transport simulation. 2.1 Room Acoustic Simulations


_Wave-based simulation._ Wave-based methods aim to simulate the

entire sound pressure field by solving the linear wave equation

numerically and include wave phenomena such as interference,

scattering and diffraction.

[Differentiable Geometric Acoustic Path Tracing using Time-Resolved Path Replay Backpropagation] - Differentiable Geometric Acoustic Path Tracing using Time-Resolved Path Replay Backpropagation

2.1 Room Acoustic Simulations


_Wave-based simulation._ Wave-based methods aim to simulate the

entire sound pressure field by solving the linear wave equation

numerically and include wave phenomena such as interference,

scattering and diffraction. Finite Element Method (FEM), Boundary

Element Method (BEM), and Finite Difference Time Domain (FDTD)

have been applied to acoustic problems [Aretz 2012; Hamilton and

Bilbao 2017; Raghuvanshi and Snyder 2014; Southern et al. 2013;

Wang et al. 2018; Ziegelwanger et al. 2015]. Although providing the

highest physical accuracy, the use of wave-based methods in room

acoustics is currently limited to rendering lower frequencies due

to their excessive memory requirements and computation times. In

addition, the boundary conditions of the differential equation, i.e.,

the acoustic impedances of the surfaces, are sometimes difficult to

specify correctly in realistic environments. _Geometrical acoustics._ Geometrical acoustics (GA) approaches ap
proximate solutions, with much higher efficiency than wave-based


methods. GA assumes that sound propagates in straight lines and

inherently neglects wave phenomena such as diffraction and inter
ference, unless these are approximated using simplified models. This

is a high-frequency approximation, where diffraction becomes less

relevant and energy-based (incoherent) summation can be assumed.

chunks.title: Differentiable Geometric Acoustic Path Tracing using Time-Resolved Path Replay Backpropagation
chunks.authors:
Ugo Finnendahl , Markus Worchel , 
Tobias Juterbock, 
Daniel Wujecki, 
Fabian Brinkmann, 
Stefan Weinzierl, Marc Alexa ( TU Berlin )
chunks.chunk_section: Differentiable Geometric Acoustic Path Tracing using Time-Resolved Path Replay Backpropagation
chunks.text:
[Differentiable Geometric Acoustic Path Tracing using Time-Resolved Path Replay Backpropagation] - Differentiable Geometric Acoustic Path Tracing using Time-Resolved Path Replay Backpropagation

This

is a high-frequency approximation, where diffraction becomes less

relevant and energy-based (incoherent) summation can be assumed. Additionally, GA methods assume a homogeneous and isotropic

medium with a constant speed of sound, and they do not account

for structure-borne sound. Despite these limitations, GA methods

are widely used in room acoustics due to their computational ef
ficiency and ability to handle complex geometry. They are partic
ularly effective for simulating sound propagation in large spaces,

such as concert halls and auditoriums, where wave effects are less

pronounced. GA approaches include the Image Source Model (ISM)

[Vorländer 2020, Ch. 11.4] and acoustic Path Tracing [Cao et al. 2016; Kiminki 2005; Schröder 2011; Siltanen et al. 2007]. The ISM

represents the analytical solution for the sound propagation of point

sources with ideal specular reflecting surfaces. Typical limitations

include the absence of scattering effects and an exponential growth

in complexity with the number of surfaces and the maximum order

of reflections, making it primarily feasible for scenarios involving

a low number of bounces or simple geometries such as a shoebox,

where no visibility checks are necessary [Allen and Berkley 1979]. Path tracing is a stochastic approach that does not suffer from the

exponential growth in complexity that ISM encounters, making it

applicable to arbitrary scene geometries.

chunks.title: Differentiable Geometric Acoustic Path Tracing using Time-Resolved Path Replay Backpropagation
chunks.authors:
Ugo Finnendahl , Markus Worchel , 
Tobias Juterbock, 
Daniel Wujecki, 
Fabian Brinkmann, 
Stefan Weinzierl, Marc Alexa ( TU Berlin )

chunks.text:
[Differentiable Geometric Acoustic Path Tracing using Time-Resolved Path Replay Backpropagation] - Differentiable Geometric Acoustic Path Tracing using Time-Resolved Path Replay Backpropagation

Path tracing is a stochastic approach that does not suffer from the

exponential growth in complexity that ISM encounters, making it

applicable to arbitrary scene geometries. It is commonly used for

simulating the diffuse late reverberation in rooms but requires a

large number of rays to adequately simulate early specular reflec
tions. Widely used room acoustical simulation software such as

RAVEN [Schröder 2011], EASE [AFMG 2023], or ODEON [Naylor

1993] use combinations of image sources and path tracing. The method presented in this paper is based on a path tracer with

no complementary ISM. _Automatic acoustic optimization._ In addition to the manual opti
mization of simulation and model parameters to achieve acoustic

goals [Labia et al. 2020] and the use of genetic algorithms [Chris
tensen et al. 2014; Pilch 2020], inverse methods have also been ap
plied in the field of room acoustics: Early work proposed an inverse

method based on the boundary element method to estimate mate
rial properties [Nava et al. 2006]. Dühring et al. [2008] minimized

include the implementation of a modular and differentiable acoustic

simulation of the wave equation, called j-Wave, by Stanziola et al. [2023]. Zhi et al. [2023] present a fully differentiable Image Source

Model, suitable for gradient-based optimization of scene parameters,

including the scene geometry – but it is limited to shoebox rooms. Our approach can optimize arbitrary scenes and parameters by

propagating derivatives through an acoustic path tracing simulation. Differentiable Geometric Acoustic Path Tracing               - 3


2.2 Differentiable Rendering


Differentiable rendering is encountered in the solution of _inverse_
_graphics problems_ : the state of a scene or more generally a system, de
fined by a set of parameters, is inferred from given observations. The

goal is to minimize the difference between renderings of the scene

and the observations. Differentiable rendering enables a gradient
based solution by making the rendering process differentiable; the

parameters are iteratively updated to minimize the difference.

The

goal is to minimize the difference between renderings of the scene

and the observations. Differentiable rendering enables a gradient
based solution by making the rendering process differentiable; the

parameters are iteratively updated to minimize the difference. _Physically-based and Approximate Methods._ Approaches to differ
entiable rendering can be categorized according to how accurately

they model energy transport. At one end are approximate methods,

where some are based on neural rendering, e.g., for 3D reconstruc
tion [Li et al. 2023; Wang et al. 2021; Worchel et al. 2022; Yariv et al. 2020] or view synthesis [Mildenhall et al. 2020]. Others use real-time

graphics techniques or simplifying assumptions for efficient, approx
imate rendering [Kerbl et al. 2023; Luan et al. 2021; Lyu et al. 2021;

Munkberg et al. 2022; Worchel and Alexa 2023]. At the other end are

physically-based methods that perform a differentiable simulation

of light transport [Jakob et al. 2022b; Li et al. 2018; Nimier-David

et al. 2019; Zhang et al. 2020]. Our approach lies at the physically-based end of the spectrum:

we perform a differentiable simulation of sound propagation, based

on the physical foundation of geometric acoustics. _Time-Dependent Energy Transport._ Many differentiable light trans
port simulations assume instantaneous energy transfer, such that

the propagation speed is ignored.
